task.name: Test processes a dev agent spawns outlive the sprint that started them and go on consuming the host indefinitely
task.story_text:
## Observed

Test processes a dev agent spawns inside its sandbox outlive the sprint that created them, and go
on consuming the machine indefinitely.

Story `issue-2284`'s dev agent ran the project's own suite four times while working, three of them
with `pytest -n auto --dist worksteal`, concurrently. Those invocations never terminated. Thirteen
hours after the sprint completed and its worktree was deleted, the machine still carried:

```
40 processes, ~321% CPU total
parent 4129   13:20:23  .venv/bin/python -m pytest tests/test_story_budget_seam.py::...
parent 68119  13:56:07  .venv/bin/python -m pytest tests/test_story_budget_seam.py -q -n auto --dist
parent 71222  13:51:50  .venv/bin/python -m pytest tests/test_story_budget_seam.py -q -n auto --dist
parent 85040  13:41:11  .venv/bin/python -m pytest tests/test_story_budget_seam.py -q
```

The parents were alive, not orphaned children of a reaped tree, and every worker executed from
`.forge/worktrees/issue-2284/.venv` — a path that no longer exists, held open by the running
processes.

The effect was not confined to wasted CPU. Every gate run on this host afterwards competed with
roughly three cores of dead test workers: a `make gate` that normally completes in about 55
seconds took 181, and a wall-clock timeout test failed inside it while passing three times out of
three when run alone. That failure was read as a possible regression in an unrelated story. Every
run duration recorded during those thirteen hours — the same durations adaptive limits derive dev
timeouts from — was measured against a host under load that nothing accounted for.

## Expected

Work a sprint starts should not outlive the sprint. A story's agent runs inside a sandbox with a
worktree, a virtualenv and a budget, all of which end when the story does; a process it spawned is
part of that same envelope and should end with it, whether the story succeeded, failed, or was
stopped.

The failure is quiet in a way that matters. A leaked process produces no artifact, no cost record
and no log line, so nothing in the run reports it and nothing in a later run knows it is there.
What it changes instead is every timing measurement taken afterwards on the same host — which is
the input the system uses to decide how long work should be allowed to take. A leak that only
wasted CPU would be a nuisance; one that silently biases the measurements the scheduler learns
from is a correctness problem for everything measured while it persists.

That an agent runs the suite at all is reasonable and worth keeping. That it can run it several
times concurrently, each fanning out across every core, inside an environment already running
under the coordinator's own parallelism, is a resource decision nobody made — the agent has no way
to know what else is executing, so the bound has to come from the side that does.

## Diagnosis

- **Observed symptom:** pytest processes spawned by a dev agent remain running and consuming CPU
  long after the sprint that started them has completed and its worktree has been removed.
- **Evidence:** four `pytest` parents with elapsed times of 13h20m–13h56m, PPIDs alive, and 40
  associated workers totalling ~321% CPU, all executing `.forge/worktrees/issue-2284/.venv/bin/python`
  after that worktree was deleted. Three carried `-n auto --dist worksteal`. The sprint that
  spawned them had completed and landed via #2285.
- **Ruled out:** not the 21-day-old orphaned `codex exec` pair from another project — those are
  idle, 13 minutes of CPU across 21 days, and unrelated.
- **Ruled out:** not a worktree-cleanup failure. The worktree was removed; the processes held the
  freed inode open, which is why they remained visible under a path that no longer resolves.
- **Confirmed cause:** processes started by an agent inside its sandbox are not part of anything
  the sprint tears down at story end, so a subprocess that does not exit on its own persists
  without limit.
- **Affected code path:** sandbox process supervision and story teardown.
- **Fix-success criterion:** a process a story's agent starts does not outlive the story, whatever
  the story's outcome, and a process that has to be terminated at teardown is recorded so the run
  shows it happened. The suite remains runnable by an agent; what it cannot do is leave work
  behind.

handoff.summary: Cycle 2 P1 was reproducible and I confirmed it by measurement before changing anything: on macOS, KERN_PROCARGS2 refuses argv/environ for SIP-protected platform binaries, so a leased /bin/sleep — the ordinary shape of a shell command — is found by no environment-token sweep. The fix steps back from the failing strategy: instead of interrogating processes after the invocation ends, the new theforge/process_tree.py observes descent while it is still knowable. A DescendantTracker walks the child links of what it already knows every 50ms, reading only ppid/pgid/start-time (which the kernel exposes for every same-uid process however hardened), remembers what it saw, and start-time-verifies every target before it is signalled so a recycled pid is never hit (#2115). A sampling pass costs 0.026ms. The lease is retained as an independent second signal because it needs no prior observation and so covers a descendant born and orphaned between two samples; its macOS enumeration moved onto the same libproc path. Both are consumed by process_group.kill_escapees, wired at all four spawn sites. Two real defects surfaced while stabilising: the lease's KERN_PROC_ALL sysctl returned ENOMEM when the table grew mid-read and reported an EMPTY process table (a sweep finding nothing exactly when the host is loaded and a leak is likeliest), and the tracker's sampling thread returned on one bad pass, blinding it for the rest of the invocation. The cycle-2 P2 is closed: gate-shell teardowns now reach the record at iterations.gate_process_teardowns — and wiring it revealed the gate shell had silently lost its tracker to an edit that stopped matching after a reformat, so that path was uncontained until now. macOS coalitions were evaluated as a kernel-maintained marker (they do survive setsid and reparenting) and rejected: a process inherits its coalition from whatever started forge, so killing by one would take the operator's shell.

acceptance_criteria.criterion: A process a story's agent starts does not outlive the story, whatever the story's outcome.
acceptance_criteria.notes: Three layers, each covering what the others cannot: the process group (verified empty at release rather than assumed from a clean exit), descendant observation (survives setsid, reparenting, an unreadable environment and env -i), and the inherited lease token (needs no prior observation, so covers a descendant born and orphaned between samples). Applied at all four spawn sites — claude, codex, gemini and the gate shell. Verified by disabling each mechanism in turn: with observation off, all three unreadable-escapee tests fail, which is the reviewer's exact repro.

acceptance_criteria.criterion: A process that has to be terminated at teardown is recorded so the run shows it happened.
acceptance_criteria.notes: Agent invocations record at cost.agents[].process_teardown, with escaped_pids separating a survivor that stayed in the group from one that left it. Gate commands now record at iterations.gate_process_teardowns, closing the cycle-2 P2 — the gate is where pytest -n auto actually runs, so it was the likeliest source of a leak with no record. Both shapes are pinned by the schema guard.

acceptance_criteria.criterion: The suite remains runnable by an agent; what it cannot do is leave work behind.
acceptance_criteria.notes: Nothing restricts what an agent may run; every clean-exit test asserts result.success is True while only the leftovers are killed. Tracked pids are start-time verified and lease tokens are per-spawn, so one invocation's teardown provably cannot reach another's work (pinned by test_a_lease_never_matches_another_spawn).

story_deviations: The cycle-2 P1 could not be fixed within the previous strategy — an environment token is unreadable for SIP-protected binaries by OS policy, not by implementation defect — so per the instruction to reconsider the approach, discovery moved from post-hoc interrogation to during-invocation observation. The plan's approach (verify the group at release, carry teardown facts into the audit) is unchanged and still the spine; this replaces only how escapees are discovered.

New module src/theforge/process_tree.py rather than growing process_group.py (convention 3): 'who descends from this spawn' is a distinct concern from process groups, sidecars and reaping, and process_group.py was already over 1100 lines.

Extended beyond the plan's file list by three adjacent paths, all for the same defect: coordinator/util.py's gate shell (flagged by both plan reviewers in cycle 0), reap_orphan_agents, and coordinator/gate.py + validate_phase.py + state.py + audit.py for the gate's audit record.

The escapee_success fake-CLI modes keep working for 0.4s after spawning. This models the actual bug (#2309's evidence was four concurrent suites run WHILE the agent worked); a CLI that spawns and exits in the same millisecond tests a race macOS gives unentitled processes no way to close, which is stated in the module docstring rather than hidden.

Regenerated the v24 schema snapshot for escaped_pids and gate_process_teardowns rather than bumping to v25: v24 is introduced by this branch and has never been written by a shipped writer, so there is no stored v24 record to migrate from.
deferred_items: Known residual, stated in the process_tree docstring rather than papered over: a descendant created AND orphaned entirely between two 50ms samples, whose environment is also unreadable, is found by neither mechanism. Closing it completely needs a kernel container — cgroup, job object, or subreaper — and macOS offers unentitled processes none. Linux could close it with PR_SET_CHILD_SUBREAPER, but that makes forge the reaper for orphaned descendants and a global waitpid would corrupt subprocess's own bookkeeping, so it was rejected as a larger change than this story.

Three existing tests had their simulated sandbox tightened to deny per-pid kills as well as killpg (test_process_group.py, test_sprint_terminal_lifecycle.py x2). The lease now ends those trees at release, so 'killpg refused' alone no longer implies survivors; denying both is what 'teardown reached only the direct child' actually means. They still exercise the reaper path.

The spec's Expected section argues an agent should not be able to run the suite several times concurrently at full fan-out and that the bound must come from the coordinator. Still not implemented: a resource-policy decision, in no acceptance criterion, and unrelated to the P1.

17 tests in test_cut_rc_isolation.py, test_sprint_lock.py and test_sprint_reexec_collision.py fail in this sandbox with PermissionError from multiprocessing.SemLock and mktemp. Pre-existing environment restriction; identical set and count across two full-suite runs before and after this iteration, and none touch changed code.

handoff.summary: Iteration 2 addressed the eight hard convention violations; the leak logic is unchanged and re-verified. The max_module_lines rule freezes any module already over 600 lines at its branch-point size, so process_group.py's +413 had to leave the file rather than be trimmed inside it — which forced the decomposition convention 3 asks for: process_lease.py (the inherited environment token), process_teardown.py (the teardown record, pure data per convention 4), and agent_sidecars.py (whether a persisted record may still be signalled), joining process_tree.py from the previous commit. process_group.py also stopped duplicating platform introspection: its kinfo_proc reader returns the same start-time values as process_tree's libproc reader (verified identical to the microsecond before consolidating), so group_members and _leader_fingerprint now delegate there — one enumeration path, one identity format. The runners split along convention 5's parsing/control seam into claude_partial_cost.py and codex_events.py. The four coordinator files had to shed exactly what I had added: a CoordinatorState field costs one line minimum, which left state.py/audit.py/validate_phase.py one line over even bare, so rather than delete unrelated code I took the alternative the cycle-2 reviewer explicitly offered and moved the gate's teardown record into the gate's own output, which lands in its trace file and the audit's output tail. That also let the schema bump go: cost.agents[].process_teardown is now written only when a kill happened, like failure_code beside it, so the record shape is unchanged and audit_substrate.py returns to v23 with no migration and no v24 snapshot. Added the four missing test mirrors (78 tests across process_tree, process_lease, agent_sidecars, process_teardown).

story_deviations: The gate-shell audit record (cycle-2 P2) moved from a CoordinatorState field to the gate's own output. Threading it through state would have required audit.py, audit_substrate.py, state.py and validate_phase.py — all frozen at their branch-point size — to grow, and a state field costs one line minimum, leaving three of them one line over even with no comment. The reviewer's finding named 'document the log line as the only record' as an acceptable resolution; this is strictly better than that, since the gate output is a durable run artifact rather than console scrollback.

The v24 schema bump and migration were reverted. Emitting process_teardown conditionally leaves the canonical record shape unchanged, so no version bump is warranted and audit_substrate.py returns to its baseline. The cost is that the teardown's nested shape is no longer pinned by the schema guard; it is pinned instead by tests/test_process_teardown.py.

Five modules were extracted beyond the plan's file list (process_lease, process_teardown, agent_sidecars, claude_partial_cost, codex_events). All are mechanical moves of existing code to satisfy the frozen-size convention, and each lands on a concern boundary the conventions already name.

Coalitions were measured and rejected: they survive setsid and reparenting, but a process inherits its coalition from whatever started forge, so killing by one would take the operator's shell.

Three test-side fixes were caused by this change and are noted so they are not read as unrelated churn: the shared killpg assertion helper lives in tests/killpg_assertions.py rather than conftest, because importing conftest by name loads it a second time and re-runs its network-guard install; two gate stubs in test_workspace_python_pin.py gained **kwargs; one contract test follows _usage_from_events to codex_events.

plan_review.findings:
- [P1-impl] [anthropic-opus-cli] Step 2 (runner_codex teardown metadata): run_in_process_group returns a subprocess.CompletedProcess (process_group.py:134), which has nowhere to carry teardown facts, and its release_group_record call is inside a finally (line 133). 'Preserve equivalent metadata from run_in_process_group(...)' therefore needs a channel the plan does not name.
  Suggestion: Dev picks the channel at implementation time — an out-parameter, a returned tuple, or a small result wrapper. Note that changing the return type would touch the two mock targets at tests/test_runner_codex.py:28 and tests/test_runner_providers.py:20, so an out-param is the cheaper shape.
- [P2] [anthropic-opus-cli] Step 3 is labeled 'action: create', but all four listed files already exist — audit_render.py, audit.py, and audit_substrate.py are modifications; only the v24 snapshot at tests/fixtures/audit_record_schema_v24.json is genuinely new.
  Suggestion: Read the step as modify-plus-one-new-snapshot. Mislabeled action only; no effect on the work.
- [P2] [anthropic-opus-cli] Step 1 blast radius: the gate's shell-timeout path at coordinator/util.py:422,455 registers a group and calls unregister_agent_group directly rather than going through release_group_record, so it will not inherit Step 1's kill-live-descendants behavior.
  Suggestion: Out of scope for the story's criteria (gate shell, not a story agent's sandbox), but worth routing through the same helper if it turns out to be cheap.
- [P2] [deepseek-deepseek-reasoner-api] Step 1 routes the new survivor-kill through the real kill_agent_group(pgid), but the existing end-to-end test test_process_group.py::test_teardown_that_leaves_survivors_records_them_and_the_reaper_uses_it monkeypatches only _killpg_for/_kill_pid to simulate a refused group kill, so under the new release semantics the real kill_agent_group would actually SIGKILL the survivor and the test's retained-sidecar/reaper assertions would fail. Similarly, the existing gemini mock tests (test_runner_gemini.py) patch theforge.runners.runner_gemini.subprocess.run and assert call args/env, which break once _run_gemini switches to run_in_process_group. Step 4 lists both test files, so the churn is anticipated, but the plan should explicitly name these two rework cases so the dev does not trip on them as regressions.
- [P2] [deepseek-deepseek-reasoner-api] The plan scopes the fix to the agent-runner boundary (claude/codex/gemini). _run_shell_detailed in coordinator/util.py — the gate-command path that also spawns pytest -n auto --dist worksteal-style trees with start_new_session=True — has the identical 'clean completion implies the group went with the child' assumption on its unregister_agent_group(pgid) path (coordinator/util.py:454-455) and is not in the plan's file list. If the acceptance criterion is read as 'any process a sprint starts', this path still leaks on clean completion; at minimum the plan should state the scope decision explicitly.
- [P1-impl] [deepseek-deepseek-reasoner-api] Step 1's clean-release kill does not reference the #2115 identity-verification discipline (leader start-time fingerprint / recorded-members snapshot) before calling kill_agent_group. In the clean-release path the risk is negligible (the pgid cannot be recycled while group_is_alive is true immediately after the leader's own wait returns), but reusing the existing _identity_verdict-style check would be the defensive move and keeps a single kill discipline. The dev can resolve this during implementation.
- [P1-impl] [deepseek-deepseek-reasoner-api] Step 2's propagation of teardown facts across run_in_process_group and _handle_exception is underspecified: run_in_process_group returns a subprocess.CompletedProcess and currently has no channel to carry release_group_record's new return value, and _handle_exception's TimeoutExpired path likewise needs a carrier (e.g. an attribute attached to the exception or CompletedProcess, or a wrapper). Both callers in the listed files make this mechanically solvable, but the concrete carrier should be chosen deliberately so _run_codex can attach metadata on the timeout path.
